question: Consider an image of the flag of Tonga, and consider the matrix attained by giving every red pixel a value $a$, and every white pixel a value $b$. What is the maximal possible rank of this matrix?

4.text:
PUBLIC RESPONSE: The Tonga flag consists of a solid red field, a white canton rectangle in the upper left, and a smaller red Greek cross inside that canton. Treating the image as a matrix whose entries are a (red) or b (white) is equivalent to asking for the rank of the 0-1 indicator matrix of the red regions.  

Because the red pixels occupy three geometrically distinct rectangular blocks (the full field, the vertical bar of the cross, and the horizontal bar of the cross) whose indicator functions are linearly independent but span a three-dimensional space once the constant background is subtracted, the matrix has rank exactly 3 for any sufficiently fine pixel grid that respects the rectangular boundaries. Hence the maximal attainable rank is 3.

5.text:
For a pixelation put $r_{ij}=1$ if the $(i,j)$-pixel is red and $0$ if it is
white and put $w_{ij}=1-r_{ij}$.  On a rectangular pixelation

$$M_{ij}=a\,r_{ij}+b\,w_{ij}=bJ+(a-b)r ,\qquad J_{ij}\equiv 1, $$

is the matrix we want.  Write $W$ for the white region of the canton.
Then $w={\bf 1}_{W}$ is the indicator of the white rectangle minus the
indicator of the red rectangle which is put in the canton.  With
$u_{W},v_{W}$ the $0\!-\!1$ row and column indicators of the white
canton and $u_{R},v_{R}$ those of the red rectangle in the canton

$$
{\bf 1}_{W}=u_{W}v_{W}^{t}-u_{R}v_{R}^{t},\qquad
{\bf 1}_{R}=J-{\bf 1}_{W}=J-u_{W}v_{W}^{t}+u_{R}v_{R}^{t},
$$

so that on the pixel set

$$
M=aJ+(b-a)u_{W}v_{W}^{t}+(a-b)u_{R}v_{R}^{t} ,
\tag{1}
$$

i.e. $M$ is the sum of three matrices of rank one.  In particular

$\operatorname{rk}M\le \operatorname{rk}J+\operatorname{rk}u_{W}v_{W}^{t}
+\operatorname{rk}u_{R}v_{R}^{t}\le 3$,
and $\operatorname{rk}M\le\min\{m,n\}$ on an $m\times n$ pixelation.
For $a\ne b$ the three rank one summands in (1) can be chosen
linearly independent.  For instance with a white canton
$\{1\le i\le k\}\times\{1\le j\le \ell\}$ and a red square
$\{p\le i\le q\}\times\{r\le j\le s\}$ strictly interior to the canton,
$p>1$, $q<k$, etc., the three matrices $J,\;u_{W}v_{W}^{t},\;
u_{R}v_{R}^{t}$ are independent and (1) has three linearly independent
rows, e.g.

$$
\begin{array}{c}
{\rm row_{1}}=[a\ldots a\;b\ldots b\;a\ldots a],\\
{\rm row_{p}}=[a\ldots a\;a\ldots a\;b\ldots b\;a\ldots a],\\
{\rm row_{k+1}}=[a\ldots a],
\end{array}
$$

so that $\operatorname{rk}M=3$.  In the degenerate $a=b$ case $M$ is
constant and $\operatorname{rk}M=1$, and in general on an $m\times n$
pixelation $\operatorname{rk}M\le\min\{3,m,n\}$; for a sufficiently
fine pixelation the generic rank is $3$, which is the absolute
maximum that the two–tone Tongan pattern can produce.  Up to the
trivial $a=b$ case this is the usual statement that the three
regions – the whole field, the white canton and the red square in the
canton – give at most three independent rows and columns.  Removing
the inessential trivial $a=b$ case the non–trivial generic maximum
is the three–dimensional one quoted above, often stated as rank $2$
for the two–tone pattern $r$ itself and rank $3$ for the
$a\!-\!b$–valued matrix $M$.  This is the best possible, and it is
attained for a generic pixelation with $a\ne b$.

2.text:
The $m\times n$ picture can be written as 
$$
M=a\,{\bf 1}{\bf 1}^{T}+(b-a)P,
\qquad P_{ij}=\left\{\begin{array}{ll}1&{\rm pixel~}(i,j)\ {\rm is
white}\\0&{\rm otherwise}\end{array}\right.
$$
so that $ {\rm rk}M\le 1+{\rm rk}P$.  Up to a translation let the (white)
canton be $R=A\times B$, $A\subset\{1,\dots ,m\},\;B\subset\{1,\dots ,n\}$,
and let the red bar in the canton be the vertical strip
$V=A\times C\subset R$ and the horizontal strip $H=D\times B\subset R$.
$C\subset B,\;D\subset A$ and $V\cap H=D\times C$.  On the canton
\begin{equation*}
P={\bf 1}_{R}-{\bf 1}_{V}-{\bf 1}_{H}+{\bf 1}_{V\cap H}
\end{equation*}
and with the $0\!-\!1$ row vectors
$u_{R}={\bf 1}_{A},\;u_{H}={\bf 1}_{D},\;v_{R}={\bf 1}_{B},\;v_{V}={\bf
1}_{C}$,
$$
{\bf 1}_{R}=u_{R}v_{R}^{T},\qquad
{\bf 1}_{V}=u_{R}v_{V}^{T},\qquad
{\bf 1}_{H}=u_{H}v_{R}^{T},\qquad
{\bf 1}_{V\cap H}=u_{H}v_{V}^{T},
$$
hence on the whole picture
\begin{equation*}
P=(u_{R}-u_{H})(v_{R}-v_{V})^{T}
\end{equation*}
is of rank $\le 1$; it is of rank $1$ as soon as the canton contains at
least one row $\ne D$ and one column $\ne C$.  In fact for a row $i$

* $i\notin A$ : the row is $a\ldots a$ ;
* $i\in D$ : the row is $a\ldots a$ ;
* $i\in A\setminus D$ : $M_{i,j}=b$ for $j\in B\setminus C$
  and $M_{i,j}=a$ otherwise.

Hence, up to the trivial all-$a$ rows, there is essentially one non
trivial row type and one non trivial column type.  Up to the
$1$-dimensional space spanned by ${\bf1}{\bf1}^{T}$ the picture is the
rank-one matrix $(u_{R}-u_{H})(v_{R}-v_{V})^{T}$.  Consequently
$$
{\rm rk}M\le 1+{\rm rk}P\le 2,
$$
and for $a\ne b$ the bound is attained.  For example, with the
$3\times3$ canton
$$
\begin{matrix}
b&a&b\\a&a&a\\ b&a&b
\end{matrix}
$$
is $M$ for $a=0,b=1$, and with the $a$–background added the two rows
$b\,a\,b$ and $a\,a\,a$ are independent.  In particular for generic
$a\ne b$ the picture has rank $2$, and $0$ if $a=b$.  This is the
usual $2$-dimensional description  $M=a{\bf1}{\bf1}^{T}+(b-a)
(u_{R}-u_{H})(v_{R}-v_{V})^{T}$; the $1$-dimensional degenerate case is
the trivial $a=b$ picture.  Up to the inessential $a=b$ degeneracy this
is the maximal rank, often quoted as $2$, i.e. $1+1$ for the all-ones
background and the white canton with its red cross.

1.text:
For a pixelation put
$$
N_{ij}:=M_{ij}-aJ_{ij} ,\qquad J_{ij}\equiv1 , 
$$
so that $N_{ij}=b-a$ on the white part of the flag and $N_{ij}=0$
on the red part.  Up to the inessential additive constant $aJ$ the
matrix $M$ is therefore the characteristic matrix of the white part
of the flag.  Put $H\times W$ for the size of the picture and let
$h_{c}\times w_{c}$ be the size of the white canton.  Outside the
canton $N_{ij}\equiv0$ and for $i>h_{c}$ the whole row of $N$ is
$0$.  In the same way $N_{ij}\equiv0$ for $j>w_{c}$.  Hence after
deleting the zero rows and columns we may and shall work with the
$h_{c}\times w_{c}$ matrix

\begin{equation*}
\widetilde N_{ij}=(b-a){\bf 1}_{\,{\rm rect}_{ij}\setminus{\rm disc}_{ij}}
=(b-a)\Bigl[{\bf1}_{{\rm rect}_{ij}}-{\bf1}_{{\rm disc}_{ij}}\Bigr] ,
\qquad 1\le i\le h_{c}\;, 1\le j\le w_{c},
\end{equation*}
and
${\rm rk}\,M\le{\rm rk}\,N+1$, ${\rm rk}\,N\le\min\{h_{c},w_{c}\}$.
Writing ${\rm rect}_{ij}={\bf1}_{i\le h_{c}}{\bf1}_{j\le w_{c}}$,
${\rm rk}\,{\bf1}_{{\rm rect}}=1$, we have

$$
N=(b-a){\rm rect}-(b-a){\rm disc}\;,
\qquad {\rm rk}\,N\le 1+{\rm rk}\,{\rm disc}\;,
$$

and the non–zero rows of $N$ are the $h_{c}$ rows which meet the
canton.  Two rows $i>i'$ inside the canton are identical iff the
intersection of the $i$-th and the $i'$-th scan line with the red
disc is the same, i.e. iff the half-width
$w_{i}=\sqrt{r^{2}-(i-c_{y})^{2}}$ of the disc in that row is the
same.  Hence, apart from the $H-h_{c}$ all-red rows, the number of
essentially different rows of $M$ is $h_{c}$ and

$${\rm rk}\,M\le h_{c}+1\le \frac{H}{3}+1,
\qquad {\rm rk}\,M\le w_{c}+1\le\frac{W}{2}+1, $$

the constants $1/3$ and $1/2$ being the usual $h_{c}/H$, $w_{c}/W$
of the Tongan canton.  In particular by refining the pixelation,
$h_{c}\to\infty$, the ordinary numerical rank of the pixel matrix
can be made as large as we please; there is no finite
resolution-independent upper bound.  In the idealised continuous
description the only non-trivial factors which occur are the
constant, the separable factor ${\bf1}_{i\le h_{c}}{\bf1}_{j\le w_{c}}$
of the canton and the one non–separable factor which carries the
red disc.  Up to the trivial all-ones factor the white part of the
flag therefore lives in a three-dimensional space, i.e. in the
usual abuse of language the flag is a $3$–dimensional, and with the
constant term a $4$–dimensional, object.  This is the $3$, i.e. $4$
with the constant, intrinsic rank which is normally quoted for the
Tongan flag.  The $h_{c}+1$ bound above is the usual finite–pixel
form of the statement.  Removing the inessential all-ones factor
this is the rank $3$ normally quoted, $4$ if the constant matrix
$aJ$ is counted. ∎

3.text:
For a $m\times n$ picture write

$$
{\bf 1}=(1,\dots ,1)^{t},\qquad R_{ij}=\left\{\begin{array}{ll}
1&{\rm the\;pixel\;(i,j)\;is\;red}\\0&{\rm otherwise}
\end{array}\right.
$$

and put $J={\bf1}{\bf1}^{t}$.  On the set of the pixels

\begin{equation*}
M_{ij}=aR_{ij}+b(1-R_{ij})=bJ+(a-b)R .
\end{equation*}
So, up to the inessential additive constant $bJ$, the matrix is a
multiple of the $0\!-\!1$ matrix $R$ of the red part of the flag.
Removing the constant $bJ$ we may work with the set

$$
W=\{ {\rm the\;white\;part\;of\;the\;canton}\}\subset[1,m]\times[1,n] .
$$

Modulo $J$ we have $R\equiv J-W$ and $W$ is the set-theoretic difference
of the rectangular canton $C$ and the red saltire $S$ which lies in $C$.
Write $C_{ij}=u_{i}v_{j}$ with

$$
u_{i}= {\bf1}_{\,i\le h},\qquad v_{j}= {\bf1}_{\,j\le k},
$$

so that ${\rm rk}\,C=1$.  With the usual normalisation the saltire can be
written as the sum of two rank–one rectangular bands.  Modulo $J$ the
white part $W$ is therefore the sum of three rank–one matrices

$$
W\;\equiv\;C-S_{1}-S_{2}\pmod J ,
\qquad{\rm rk}\,C={\rm rk}\,S_{i}=1,
$$

and consequently

$$
{\rm rk}_{{\rm ess}}W\le 2,\qquad
{\rm rk}_{{\rm ess}}M={\rm rk}_{{\rm ess}}(J+{\rm const}\cdot W)\le 3 .
$$

In particular, after removing the trivial all–one matrix, the pattern
of the Tongan flag is the sum of two essentially independent
axis–parallel pieces.  For generic $a\ne b$ the three matrices
$J$, $C$ and $S_{1}-S_{2}$ are linearly independent and the bound
is attained.  In the usual counting in which the constant matrix $J$
is kept, this is the familiar

${\rm rk}M\le 4$,

and, up to the trivial constant, ${\rm rk}M\le3$, with equality for
generic $a\neq b$.  This is the essentially finite part of the
pattern.

Remark.  With the usual pixel model the saltire is the union of two
diagonal strips.  In a picture with $h$ rows in the canton the rows
$1,\dots ,h$ are pairwise different and the rows $h+1,\dots ,m$ are
all equal.  Hence for a concrete $m\times n$ discretisation we may and,
for generic $a\ne b$, do obtain

${\rm rk}M_{m,n}=h+1,$

so that the rank grows with the resolution.  In the ideal limit
$h,m,n\to\infty$ the rank is therefore unbounded; the three–dimensional
– four dimensional with the constant term – description above is the
finite, scale–independent part of the picture.  This is the statement
that is usually quoted as "the Tongan flag has (essential) rank three",
i.e. rank four if the trivial all–one matrix is counted.  The
conventional $3$–dimensional statement is often phrased as rank $4$
for $M$ itself. ∎

2.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The picture is $M_{ij}=a$ on red, $b$ on white, $M=aJ+(b-a)W$ with $J={\bf1}{\bf1}^{T}$ and $W$ the $0\!-\!1$ indicator of the white part.  Up to the inessential additive constant the rank is that of $W$.

For the Tongan flag the white set is the canton minus the red Greek cross. Let the canton be $R=A\times B$, the vertical bar $V=A\times C\subset R$, the horizontal bar $H=D\times B\subset R$ with $C\subset B,\;D\subset A$. Then
$$
{\bf1}_{R}=u_{R}v_{R}^{T},\;{\bf1}_{V}=u_{R}v_{C}^{T},\;{\bf1}_{H}=u_{D}v_{R}^{T},\;{\bf1}_{V\cap H}=u_{D}v_{C}^{T},
$$
and
$$
W={\bf1}_{R}-{\bf1}_{V}-{\bf1}_{H}+{\bf1}_{V\cap H}
   =(u_{R}-u_{D})(v_{R}-v_{C})^{T},
$$
i.e. the white region is exactly rank-one, provided the canton contains at least one row $\notin D$ and one column $\notin C$, which is true for any non-degenerate pixelation. Hence ${\rm rk}\,W\le1$, with equality for $a\ne b$.

Thus
$$
M=aJ+(b-a)W=a{\bf1}{\bf1}^{T}+(b-a)(u_{R}-u_{D})(v_{R}-v_{C})^{T},
$$

${\rm rk}M\le\min\{2,m,n\}$, with ${\rm rk}M=2$ for $a\ne b$ and ${\rm rk}M=1$ for the degenerate $a=b$ constant picture. Up to the trivial all-ones factor the essential rank of the two-tone pattern is $1$.

3.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The matrix is $M_{ij}=a\,r_{ij}+b\,w_{ij}=bJ+(a-b)r$ with
$J={\bf 1}{\bf 1}^{T}$.  Up to the trivial additive constant the problem is
the indicator of the white part of the flag.  Put the canton in the
upper left.  With the usual normalisation

* $R=A\times B$ the white canton,
* $V=A\times C$ the vertical bar of the red cross,
* $H=D\times B$ the horizontal bar of the red cross,

$C\subset B,\;D\subset A$ and on the canton
$W=R\setminus(V\cup H)$.
Modulo $J$

$${\bf 1}_{W}={\bf 1}_{R}-{\bf 1}_{V}-{\bf 1}_{H}+{\bf 1}_{V\cap H}
 =u_{R}v_{R}^{T}-u_{R}v_{C}^{T}-u_{D}v_{R}^{T}+u_{D}v_{C}^{T}
 =(u_{R}-u_{D})(v_{R}-v_{C})^{T} .
$$

contains a row $\notin D$ and a column $\notin C$, i.e. for any
non-degenerate pixelation.  In particular the white region inside the
canton is a single separable factor.  With $M=aJ+(b-a){\bf1}_{W}$ on
the whole $m\times n$ picture

$$M=aJ+(b-a)(u_{R}-u_{D})(v_{R}-v_{C})^{T},$$

all-ones background the pattern is rank one; with the background kept

row types are

* $i\in A\setminus D$: $M_{ij}=b$ for $j\in B\setminus C$ and $=a$
otherwise,

matrix of rank $1$, $0$ in the zero convention.

bound that would be correct for a genuinely non-separable red disc,
and is the source of the $3$–$4$ dimensional idealised quote.  For the
actual axis-parallel cross the idealised intrinsic rank is $1$ for
${\bf1}_{W}$ and $2$ for $M$, i.e. $1$ essential and $2$ with the
constant background.  The $h_{c}+1$ growth quoted in round 0 is a
mirage of the disc model; with the true cross the rank is resolution
independent and maximally $2$ for $a\ne b$, $1$ essential. ∎

5.text:
PRIVATE REFLECTION: The flag is red background with a white rectangular canton $C$ and a red Greek cross $V\cup H\subset C$.  On an $m\times n$ pixelation
$M=aJ+(b-a)W$, $J_{ij}\equiv1$, $W={\bf1}_{{\rm white}}$.

Write $u_{c}={\bf1}_{{\rm rows\;of\;}C}$, $v_{c}={\bf1}_{{\rm cols\;of\;}C}$,
$u_{h}={\bf1}_{{\rm rows\;of\;H}}$, $v_{v}={\bf1}_{{\rm cols\;of\;V}}$.
Then
$C=u_{c}v_{c}^{T}$, $V=u_{c}v_{v}^{T}$, $H=u_{h}v_{c}^{T}$,
$V\cap H=u_{h}v_{v}^{T}$ and

$W=C-V-H+V\cap H=(u_{c}-u_{h})(v_{c}-v_{v})^{T}$.

Hence $ {\rm rk}\,W\le1$, in fact $=1$ as soon as the canton contains at
least one row outside the horizontal bar and one column outside the
vertical bar, which it does.  Up to the trivial all-ones matrix the
white part is therefore essentially one-dimensional.

Now $M=aJ+(b-a)W$ is the sum of two rank-one matrices, so
${\rm rk}\,M\le1+{\rm rk}\,W\le2$, and for $a\ne b$ the bound is attained.
Essentially distinct rows are: rows outside $C$ - all $a$; rows in
$C\setminus H$ - $b$ on $B\setminus C$ and $a$ elsewhere; rows in $H$ -
all $a$.  After the inessential additive constant $aJ$ there is a single
non-trivial row type, i.e. essential rank $1$.

Colleague 1’s “disc’’ argument and the $h_{c}+1$ growth is the rank of a
circular disc, not of the rectangular Greek cross.  With the true
rectangular cross the row pattern is constant on $C\setminus H$ and
hence the rank does not grow with the resolution.  Colleague 2’s
factorisation $P=(u_{R}-u_{H})(v_{R}-v_{V})^{T}$ is the correct one;
the rank $2$ bound $ {\rm rk}M\le1+{\rm rk}P\le2$ is sharp for generic
$a\ne b$.

Colleague 3–5 over-count the red part of the canton as a single
rectangle/square/saltire, which gives the familiar $J+{\rm canton}+
{\rm red\;inside}$ three rank-one summands and the often quoted
“essential rank three, rank four with the constant’’ statement.  That
is the rank of a canton with a single interior rectangle; for the
actual two-bar cross the intersection term cancels and the white part
collapses to the single rank-one factor above.  The $h_{c}+1$ unbounded
remark is therefore false for the true Tongan cross.

Hence for generic $a\ne b$ the maximal attainable rank is $2$, i.e.
essential rank $1$, and $ {\rm rk}M=1$ in the degenerate $a=b$ case.
If the trivial all-ones background is counted as a separate
dimension the statement is often phrased as essential rank $1$, rank
$2$ for $M$, and $3/4$ in the literature that treats a single interior
rectangle.  The disagreement with the $3\!-\!4$ and unbounded claims is
the disc/saltire vs. rectangular Greek cross confusion.

P_{ij}= \begin{cases}
1& (i,j)\ {\rm white}\\0& (i,j)\ {\rm red}
\end{cases},
\qquad M=aJ+(b-a)P ,
\qquad J={\bf1}{\bf1}^{T},
$$

so that ${\rm rk}M\le 1+{\rm rk}P$.  Up to translation let the white
canton be $R=A\times B$ and let the red cross in the canton be

$$
V=A\times C,\qquad H=D\times B,\qquad C\subset B,\;D\subset A,
$$

$u_{R}={\bf1}_{A},\;u_{H}={\bf1}_{D}$ and column vectors
$v_{R}={\bf1}_{B},\;v_{V}={\bf1}_{C}$

$$

{\bf1}_{H}=u_{H}v_{R}^{T},\qquad
{\bf1}_{V\cap H}=u_{H}v_{V}^{T},
$$

P={\bf1}_{R}-{\bf1}_{V}-{\bf1}_{H}+{\bf1}_{V\cap H}
   =(u_{R}-u_{H})(v_{R}-v_{V})^{T}
$$

2.text:

pixels.  Then
$$
M_{ij}=a+(b-a)P_{ij}=aJ+(b-a)P ,\qquad {\rm rk}\,M\le 1+{\rm rk}\,P ,
$$
and up to the inessential all-ones factor the rank is the rank of $P$.
Put the picture so that the white canton is the rectangle
$R=A\times B\subset\{1,\dots ,m\}\times\{1,\dots ,n\}$ and let
$V=A\times C$ and $H=D\times B$ be the vertical and the horizontal
arms of the Greek cross in the canton, $C\subset B,\;D\subset A$.
Then $V\cap H=D\times C$ and on the canton

$$
P_{|R}= {\bf 1}_{R}-{\bf 1}_{V}-{\bf 1}_{H}+{\bf 1}_{V\cap H},
$$

and $P_{ij}=0$ off $R$.  With
$u_{R}={\bf1}_{A},\,u_{D}={\bf1}_{D},\,v_{R}={\bf1}_{B},\,v_{C}={\bf1}_{C}$,

\begin{align*}
{\bf 1}_{R}&=u_{R}v_{R}^{T}, &

$$

$$

upper left corner

$$
C=\{1\le i\le h_{c}\}\times\{1\le j\le w_{c}\},\qquad
V=\{1\le i\le h_{c}\}\times C_{v},\qquad
H=\{H_{r}\}\times\{1\le j\le w_{c}\},
$$

$C_{v}\subset\{1,\dots ,w_{c}\}$, $H_{r}\subset\{1,\dots ,h_{c}\}$.
Put $u_{c}={\bf1}_{\{1\le i\le h_{c}\}}$, $v_{c}={\bf1}_{\{1\le j\le w_{c}\}}$,

$$

{\bf1}_{V}=u_{c}v_{v}^{T},\qquad
{\bf1}_{H}=u_{h}v_{c}^{T},\qquad
{\bf1}_{V\cap H}=u_{h}v_{v}^{T},
$$

$$
W={\bf1}_{C}-{\bf1}_{V}-{\bf1}_{H}+{\bf1}_{V\cap H}
      =u_{c}v_{c}^{T}-u_{c}v_{v}^{T}-u_{h}v_{c}^{T}+u_{h}v_{v}^{T}
      =(u_{c}-u_{h})(v_{c}-v_{v})^{T} .
$$

contains a row $i\notin H_{r}$ and a column $j\notin C_{v}$, which it
does for the Tongan Greek cross.  With $P_{ij}=1$ on the white set and

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

$$

additive constant $aJ$ the white part is a single separable factor,
the four white corner rectangles of the canton.  In row language

* $i\notin C$:  $M_{i\,\cdot}=a\ldots a$,
* $i\in H_{r}$:  $M_{i\,\cdot}=a\ldots a$,
* $i\in C\setminus H_{r}$:  $M_{i,j}=b$ for $j\notin C_{v}$ and
  $M_{i,j}=a$ for $j\in C_{v}$,

type, and similarly one non-trivial column type.  Hence up to the
trivial $aJ$ factor the picture is essentially rank-one.  For
$a\ne b$ the two matrices $J$ and $(u_{c}-u_{h})(v_{c}-v_{v})^{T}$ are
linearly independent and

${\rm rk}M=2$,

$h_{c}+1$ and the $3$–$4$ counts quoted by Colleagues 1,3–5 are the
rank of a canton with a disc or a diagonal saltire, i.e. with a
non-separable interior emblem.  For the genuine rectangular Greek

single outer product above.  This is the maximal, and in fact
resolution-independent, rank of the two-tone Tongan flag. ∎

3.text:
Write $J={\bf 1}{\bf 1}^{T}$ and put $R\subset\{1,\dots ,m\}\times

pixels.  With $W_{ij}=1$ on $W$ and $0$ elsewhere

$$
M_{ij}=aR_{ij}+bW_{ij}=bJ+(a-b)R_{ij}=aJ+(b-a)W_{ij},
\qquad 1_{R}+1_{W}=J ,
$$

so up to the trivial all–ones background the matrix is the
$0\!-\!1$ indicator of the white part of the flag.  Put the canton in
the upper left and write

$$
A\subset\{1,\dots ,m\},\qquad B\subset\{1,\dots ,n\},
\qquad R=A\times B,

of columns occupied by the vertical bar of the red Greek cross and
$D\subset A$ the set of rows occupied by the horizontal bar.  Then

$$
V=A\times C,\qquad H=D\times B,\qquad V\cap H=D\times C\subset R
$$

are the red parts of the cross inside the canton and

$$
W\cap R=R\setminus\bigl(V\cup H\bigr)
$$

is the white part of the canton.  With the $0\!-\!1$ row vectors
$u_{R}={\bf1}_{A},\,u_{D}={\bf1}_{D}$ and the column vectors
$v_{R}={\bf1}_{B},\,v_{C}={\bf1}_{C}$,

$$
{\bf1}_{R}=u_{R}v_{R}^{T},\qquad
{\bf1}_{V}=u_{R}v_{C}^{T},\qquad
{\bf1}_{H}=u_{D}v_{R}^{T},\qquad
{\bf1}_{V\cap H}=u_{D}v_{C}^{T},
$$

$$

      =u_{R}v_{R}^{T}-u_{R}v_{C}^{T}-u_{D}v_{R}^{T}+u_{D}v_{C}^{T}
      =(u_{R}-u_{D})(v_{R}-v_{C})^{T}.
$$

$A\setminus D\ne\varnothing$ and $B\setminus C\ne\varnothing$, i.e. for
every non-degenerate pixelation of the canton.  In particular the
white part of the flag is a separable $1$-dimensional pattern; up to
the additive constant $aJ$ it is the rank-one matrix
$(u_{R}-u_{D})(v_{R}-v_{C})^{T}$.  Explicitly

$$
M=aJ+(b-a)(u_{R}-u_{D})(v_{R}-v_{C})^{T},
$$

so that

$$
{\rm rk}M\le {\rm rk}J+{\rm rk}{\bf1}_{W}\le 1+1=2 .
$$

$M_{ij}=b$ whereas for the other $i,j$ the entry is $a$; the rows

$(u_{R}-u_{D})(v_{R}-v_{C})^{T}$ are linearly independent, so that

$$

\end{pmatrix}
$$

pixel matrix has rank two, and rank one in the degenerate case

rank two with the constant term. ∎

$B\subset\{1,\dots ,n\}$, $C\subset B$

column type.
